sections.html:
In Camden the quickest sale is a cash purchase from a buyer who accepts the house as it is and handles the city's sale certificate. A listing can work for houses in good shape in neighborhoods with active demand, but the city's resale rules add steps whichever way you go. Selling yourself without an agent is allowed, with the same paperwork.

Camden is the county seat on the Delaware River, directly across from Philadelphia, with 71,430 residents.

Camden values sit far below the rest of the Philadelphia area. The median owner-occupied value is $112,000, median gross rent is $1,226, and just 34.4% of the city's 24,443 households own. Median household income is $40,546, so many sellers are carrying a house they cannot afford to repair, or an heir inheriting one.

The most common housing type is the rowhouse. The city recognizes more than 20 neighborhoods, including Cooper Grant, Cramer Hill, East Camden, Parkside, Waterfront South, Rosedale, Pyne Point and Gateway.

  • Rowhouses share walls and roofs, so a buyer's inspection will look closely at party walls and roof drainage.
  • Vacant or fire-damaged houses can still sell, but the buyer may sign an agreement not to occupy until permits are closed.
  • Homes near the waterfront, the Rutgers campus and the hospital district sit close to the city's largest employers.

Transit is a real selling point. The PATCO Speedline runs 24 hours to Philadelphia and to Collingswood, Haddonfield, Cherry Hill and Lindenwold, and NJ Transit's River Line light rail runs from Camden to Trenton with four stops in the city. The Walter Rand Transportation Center at Martin Luther King Boulevard and Broadway joins PATCO, River Line and NJ Transit buses. By road, Interstate 676 and U.S. 30 lead to the Benjamin Franklin Bridge. Mean travel time to work is 23.8 minutes.

Camden City School District runs 19 schools, and charter and renaissance schools operate alongside it, which buyers with children will ask about.

Camden requires a Certificate of Continued Occupancy (the building bureau also calls it a Camden Resale Occupancy Certificate) to be applied for and issued before any property in the city is sold or conveyed. The seller is responsible for applying, though the buyer may apply with the seller's written permission. The certificate is issued to the buyer, not the seller. If a buyer closes without one, the buyer stays liable for penalties of up to $2,000 until it issues.

The process starts with a zoning permit at City Hall, then an application to the Construction and Building Bureau, followed by four inspections: building, plumbing, electric and fire. All open building permits must be closed first. If the house is not habitable, the buyer can sign an Agreement to Not Occupy and commit to pulling permits and doing the work. Plan submissions are digital only. A change of tenant in a rental is a different step and goes through the Housing Department.

Camden occupancy certificate costs and rules
RequirementAmount or rule
Certificate of Continued Occupancy application$200
Fire safety inspection fee (separate)$64
Application validity6 months, then a new application unless permits are open
Penalty if buyer closes without a certificateUp to $2,000
Annual rent control registration, per rental unit$25

The Bureau of Housing enforces the city's property maintenance code. Rental properties must be inspected at a change of ownership or occupancy and hold a Rental Approval Certificate before anyone moves in, and buildings with three or more units need a license. To schedule an inspection, all taxes must be current, utilities must be on, the fee is paid when scheduling, and the property must be registered with both the Rent Control office and the Municipal Clerk.

The city has had a rent control ordinance since March 12, 1981. At lease expiration a landlord may raise rent by no more than the lower of the 12-month average consumer price index for the Philadelphia area or 6% of the latest rent, and rent cannot rise during a lease. A buyer of a rental building takes on those limits, so a landlord selling should have the registration file ready.

sections.h2: Taxes and state fees when selling in Camden
sections.html:
The Office of Assessments maintains the tax map, processes senior and veteran deductions and exemptions, receives abatement requests, and handles assessment appeals filed with the Camden County Board of Taxation or the New Jersey Tax Court. The office is in City Hall, Room 329, at 520 Market Street. Check that taxes are current before listing, since a lien can hold up a closing.

New Jersey's Realty Transfer Fee falls on the seller. At Camden-level prices below $350,000, the schedule is $2.00 per $500 on the first $150,000, $3.35 per $500 from $150,000 to $200,000 and $3.90 per $500 above that. Senior citizens, blind or disabled sellers and certain low and moderate income housing sales qualify for lower rates, starting at $0.50 per $500 on the first $150,000. Ask your attorney which rate applies to you.

sections.h2: How a cash sale fits Camden's rules
sections.html:
A cash buyer can take on the certificate process, which suits vacant, damaged or inherited houses. Settle in writing who applies, who pays the $200 application and the $64 fire fee, and who closes any open permits. If the house is not habitable, the Agreement to Not Occupy lets the buyer proceed while the work is done.

Compare a cash offer with what a listing would net after commission, repairs and the months you would carry taxes and utilities. Before you sign, have a New Jersey attorney read the contract and confirm how the certificate and any penalty are handled.

For a quick start, confirm that taxes are current, look up open permits with the Construction and Building Bureau and gather your deed. If tenants live in the house, bring the Rent Control registration and the Rental Approval Certificate so the buyer sees a clean file.

Expect the four inspections (building, plumbing, electric and fire) to be booked separately, so ask each inspector for a date as soon as the zoning permit is in hand. If an inspection fails, fix the listed items and request a repeat visit before the six-month application window runs out. On closing day your attorney confirms the certificate is in the buyer's name, pays off any lien and records the deed.

faqs.q: Who applies for the Certificate of Continued Occupancy in Camden?
faqs.a: The seller. The buyer may file as the seller's agent with written permission, but the certificate is issued to the buyer. The application costs $200 plus a separate $64 fire safety fee.

faqs.q: How long is a Camden occupancy certificate application good for?
faqs.a: Six months. After that a new application must be filed and paid for, unless there are open permits on the property.

faqs.q: Can I sell a vacant or damaged house in Camden?
faqs.a: Yes. If the house is not habitable, the buyer can sign an Agreement to Not Occupy and then obtain permits, do the work and apply for the certificate. Open permits have to be closed before a certificate issues.

faqs.q: Is there rent control in Camden?
faqs.a: Yes. Camden has had a rent control ordinance since 1981, with a cap at the lower of the Philadelphia-area consumer price index or 6% at lease expiration, and landlords register each rental unit annually for $25.

faqs.q: Where do I appeal a Camden property assessment?
faqs.a: Appeals go to the Camden County Board of Taxation or the New Jersey Tax Court. The Office of Assessments, at 520 Market Street, Room 329, can explain the process and handles deductions.
